stem: A business states it can lose at most 15 minutes of transaction data in a disaster. Which recovery metric does this statement BEST define?

options.rationale: RPO measures the maximum acceptable data loss, expressed as how far back in time to the last good recovery point, which matches the 15-minute limit.
RTO measures time to restore systems, not the amount of data loss tolerated.
MTD is the maximum outage duration, not the data-loss tolerance.
WRT is the post-restore validation/reintegration time, unrelated to data-loss tolerance.

stem: A team commits to having a downed system technically restored within 4 hours of an outage. Which metric does this target BEST define?

options.rationale: RTO is the target time to restore a system after disruption, which the 4-hour commitment describes.
RPO measures acceptable data loss, not the time to restore the system.
MTBF is a reliability metric for expected time between failures, not a recovery target.
ALE is a quantitative risk metric for expected yearly loss, not a recovery time.

stem: A function has an MTD of 8 hours. The proposed RTO is 4 hours and WRT is 3 hours. Which conclusion is MOST accurate?

options.text: The plan is viable because RTO + WRT (7 hours) is within the 8-hour MTD
options.rationale: RTO plus WRT must not exceed MTD; 7 hours fits within 8 hours, leaving a margin.

options.text: The plan fails because RTO alone exceeds MTD
options.rationale: RTO is 4 hours, well under the 8-hour MTD, so RTO alone does not exceed it.

options.text: MTD is irrelevant to RTO and WRT
options.rationale: MTD is the outer bound that RTO + WRT must fit within, so it is directly relevant.

options.text: WRT should be ignored when checking against MTD
options.rationale: WRT must be added to RTO when comparing to MTD; ignoring it can hide an overrun.

stem: A system has an RPO of only a few minutes. Which backup/replication approach BEST satisfies this?

options.rationale: A minutes-level RPO cannot tolerate gaps, so continuous replication/journaling is required to limit data loss to minutes.
Nightly backups can lose up to a day of data, far exceeding a few-minute RPO.
Weekly backups could lose up to a week of data, grossly violating the RPO.
Monthly exports provide an extremely poor RPO, unacceptable here.

stem: Which statement BEST describes the relationship between disaster recovery (DR) and business continuity (BC)?

options.text: DR focuses on restoring IT systems and is a subset of the broader BC effort to sustain the business
options.rationale: DR is the tactical, technology-focused recovery of systems within the wider strategic BC framework.

options.text: BC is a subset of DR
options.rationale: This reverses the relationship; DR is the subset, BC is the broader effort.

options.text: DR and BC are entirely unrelated
options.rationale: They are closely related; DR executes within BC.

options.text: DR replaces the need for BC
options.rationale: DR restores systems but does not sustain the entire business, so it does not replace BC.

stem: A fire strikes the data center during business hours. In executing the DR plan, what must be prioritized FIRST?

options.text: The safety and evacuation of personnel
options.rationale: Life safety always takes precedence over any asset or system recovery in DR.
System recovery is important but never comes before protecting human life.
Hardware salvage is secondary to protecting people.
Communications matter but do not take priority over immediate life safety.

stem: After systems are technically restored, the team still needs time to validate data, reconfigure integrations, and reconnect users before real work resumes. Which metric BEST captures this period?

options.rationale: WRT is the time after technical restore needed to validate and reintegrate systems so business work can resume.
RPO concerns data-loss tolerance, not post-restore validation time.
MTD is the overall outage limit, not the specific post-restore work period.
MTTR is an average repair-time reliability metric, not the DR reintegration window.

stem: In the DR process, when does restoration to the primary site BEST occur?

options.text: After critical operations are stable at the alternate site and the primary is validated as safe
options.rationale: Restoration returns operations to the primary environment only once it is safe and validated and critical operations are already stable.

options.text: Before assessing the damage to the primary site
options.rationale: Moving back before damage assessment risks returning to an unsafe or nonfunctional site.
Recovery of critical systems precedes restoration to the primary; jumping to restoration first is out of order.

options.text: Never, once at an alternate site the primary is abandoned
options.rationale: Restoration to a permanent/primary environment is the intended end state, not permanent alternate operation.

stem: What does Maximum Tolerable Downtime (MTD) represent?

options.text: The longest a function can be unavailable before causing unacceptable harm
options.rationale: MTD is the outer limit of downtime a business function can endure before serious or irreparable harm results.

options.text: The amount of data that can be lost
options.rationale: That describes RPO, not MTD.

options.text: The time to validate systems after restore
options.rationale: That describes WRT, not MTD.
Scan frequency is unrelated to MTD.

stem: A proposed RTO for a function is longer than its MTD. Which conclusion is MOST accurate?

options.text: The RTO is invalid because it must be shorter than the MTD
options.rationale: RTO must fit within MTD; an RTO exceeding MTD means the function would be down past its tolerable limit.

options.text: The RTO is fine because RTO can exceed MTD
options.rationale: RTO exceeding MTD violates the required relationship and leaves the business exposed beyond tolerance.

options.text: MTD should be lowered to match the RTO
options.rationale: MTD is set by business impact, not adjusted to accommodate an overlong RTO.

options.text: RPO should be ignored to fix the problem
options.rationale: RPO is a separate data-loss metric and ignoring it does not resolve the RTO-versus-MTD conflict.

stem: An executive asks, 'How much recent data are we willing to lose if we fail over?' Which metric MOST directly answers this question?

options.rationale: RPO defines the maximum acceptable data loss, exactly what the executive is asking about.
RTO answers how quickly systems are restored, not how much data may be lost.
WRT is post-restore validation time, not a data-loss measure.
MTD is the outage limit, not the data-loss tolerance.

stem: An executive asks, 'How fast can we get the system running again after it goes down?' Which metric MOST directly answers this?

options.rationale: RTO is the target time to restore a system after a disruption, which answers how fast recovery occurs.
RPO concerns data-loss tolerance, not the speed of restoring the system.
ARO is a risk frequency metric, not a recovery timing measure.
EF is a percentage-of-loss risk metric, unrelated to recovery time.

stem: A function's MTD is 6 hours. The team's RTO is 5 hours and WRT is 3 hours. What does this BEST indicate about the plan?

options.text: The plan fails because RTO + WRT (8 hours) exceeds the 6-hour MTD
options.rationale: Since RTO plus WRT must fit within MTD, 8 hours exceeding 6 hours means the business would be down beyond tolerance.

options.text: The plan succeeds because RTO alone is under MTD
options.rationale: RTO alone is not the test; RTO + WRT must be within MTD, and here it is not.

options.text: WRT does not count toward downtime
options.rationale: WRT is part of the downtime before work resumes and must be included.

options.text: MTD should be increased to 8 hours to fit
options.rationale: MTD is dictated by business impact, not raised to accommodate a plan that overruns.

stem: A business sets an RPO of zero (no acceptable data loss). Which approach is MOST consistent with meeting it?

options.text: Synchronous replication that commits data to a second location before acknowledging writes
options.rationale: A zero RPO requires that no committed transaction be lost, which synchronous replication provides by writing to two locations together.
Daily backups can lose up to a day of data, incompatible with a zero RPO.
Weekly backups could lose a week of data, far from zero.
No protection guarantees data loss, the opposite of a zero RPO.

stem: Which activity is MOST characteristic of disaster recovery specifically rather than the broader business continuity effort?

options.text: Restoring failed servers and databases at an alternate site
options.rationale: Restoring IT systems and infrastructure is the tactical, technology-focused work that defines disaster recovery.

options.text: Determining overall business criticality and strategy for the whole enterprise
options.rationale: Enterprise-wide criticality and strategy are business continuity concerns, broader than DR.
Long-term mission-setting is a governance/strategic activity, not DR.
Budget approval is unrelated to disaster recovery of systems.

stem: During a disaster, keeping employees, customers, and regulators informed through predefined channels is handled by which DR consideration?

options.text: The communications component of the DR plan
options.rationale: Predefined communications keep internal and external stakeholders informed during and after a disaster.
RPO measures data-loss tolerance, not stakeholder communication.
RAID is disk fault tolerance, unrelated to communications.
The CAB governs planned changes, not disaster communications.

stem: After the immediate response and ensuring personnel are safe, what should the DR team do FIRST to guide the recovery effort?

options.text: Assess the scope and severity of the damage and what must be recovered
options.rationale: Damage assessment determines what is affected and drives the recovery priorities and actions.

options.text: Immediately restore all systems to the primary site
options.rationale: Restoring to the primary before assessing damage risks returning to an unsafe or broken environment.

options.text: Cancel the DR plan to save money
options.rationale: Abandoning the plan during a disaster leaves recovery unmanaged.

options.text: Delete all backups to start fresh
options.rationale: Deleting backups destroys the means of recovery.

stem: Which relationship among the recovery metrics is correctly stated?

options.text: RTO + WRT must not exceed MTD
options.rationale: Total time to restore systems (RTO) plus validate/reintegrate them (WRT) must fit within the maximum tolerable downtime.

options.text: MTD must be shorter than RTO
options.rationale: This reverses the relationship; RTO must be shorter than MTD, not the other way around.
RPO (data loss) and RTO (recovery time) measure different things and are not equal by definition.

options.text: WRT must be longer than MTD
options.rationale: WRT is only part of the recovery time and must fit within MTD, not exceed it.

stem: In any disaster recovery scenario, which consideration MOST consistently takes precedence over all others?

options.rationale: Life safety is always the top priority, ahead of any asset or system recovery.
Revenue systems matter but never come before human safety.
Marketing materials are low priority relative to life safety.
Data-loss goals are important but subordinate to protecting people.

stem: Which statement about RTO and RPO is LEAST accurate?

options.text: RTO measures acceptable data loss while RPO measures time to restore systems
options.rationale: This is the reversed (incorrect) definition; RTO is recovery time and RPO is data-loss tolerance, so the statement is least accurate.

options.text: RTO is the target time to restore a system after disruption
options.rationale: This correctly defines RTO, so it is accurate.

options.text: RPO is the maximum acceptable amount of data loss
options.rationale: This correctly defines RPO, so it is accurate.

options.text: RPO influences how frequently data must be backed up or replicated
options.rationale: This is an accurate implication of RPO, so it is not the least accurate statement.
